paragraphs.text: Amazon is in advanced talks to acquire Decart, a San Francisco artificial intelligence startup, in a deal that would value the company at roughly $7.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on November 21, 2026, citing people familiar with the matter. According to the report, an agreement could be announced as soon as the following week, although the negotiations could still break down.
An Amazon spokesperson declined to comment when asked about the talks, PYMNTS reported. No statement from Decart was available in the coverage.

Decart was founded in 2023. PYMNTS, summarizing the Financial Times report, described its software as a way to let AI models work more efficiently and free up capacity on computer chips. Earlier coverage described the same technology as helping AI models run on different kinds of chips, including Amazon's own Trainium processors.

According to the Financial Times account cited by PYMNTS, Decart was an early adopter of Trainium. Amazon introduced its Trainium3 chip late last year as an alternative to the graphics processors sold by Nvidia, which dominate the market for training and running large AI models.
A deal that has been building for weeks

The talks are not new. In October, The Wall Street Journal reported that Amazon was discussing a purchase of Decart at a valuation of around $7 billion, as covered at the time by GeekWire and The Seattle Times, and PYMNTS noted that earlier report in its own coverage. The new figure reported by the Financial Times is about half a billion dollars higher.

Amazon is not the first large AI company to look at Decart. Anthropic was reported earlier in 2026 as a possible buyer before it walked away from a deal, according to PYMNTS and earlier reporting by GeekWire.

For Amazon Web Services, the value of Decart appears to lie less in a consumer product and more in software that makes its own chips easier to use. Cloud customers often stay with Nvidia hardware because their models and tools are built for it. Software that moves AI work onto Trainium with little effort could lower that barrier, and PYMNTS framed the purchase as part of Amazon's effort to compete with Nvidia. Paying several billion dollars for a company that is only three years old would also show how much large cloud providers are willing to spend to reduce their dependence on a single chip supplier.

The next step to watch is a formal announcement from Amazon or Decart, which would confirm the price and the terms. After that, attention will turn to any review by competition regulators and to whether Decart's software starts showing up as part of the AI services that Amazon Web Services sells to its cloud customers.
